paragraphs: A man who has at last found something to do will not need a new suit for it; his old one will serve, though it has lain dusty in the attic for years. Old shoes will last a hero longer than his valet, if a hero ever has a valet. Bare feet are older than shoes, and he can make them do. Only those who attend soirées and legislative halls need new coats, changed as often as the men inside them change. But if my clothes are fit to worship God in, they will do, will they not? Who has ever worn out his old coat so completely that giving it to a poor boy was no longer an act of charity? That boy might pass it on to someone poorer still, or perhaps richer, who could do with less. Beware, Thoreau says, of all enterprises that require new clothes rather than a new wearer of clothes. Without a new man, how can the new clothes be made to fit? Whatever enterprise lies before you, try it in your old clothes. What men want is not something to do with, but something to do, or rather something to be. Perhaps we should never acquire a new suit, however ragged the old, until we have acted or ventured so that we feel like new men in it. Keeping it then would be like keeping new wine in old bottles. Our moulting season, like that of birds, must be a crisis in our lives. The loon withdraws to solitary ponds to pass it. Likewise the snake casts off its skin and the caterpillar its coat, through inner effort and expansion, for clothes are merely our outermost layer. Otherwise we shall be found sailing under false colours, and finally be condemned by our own opinion and by that of mankind.

We add garment after garment, as if we grew like certain plants only by addition from outside. Our outer clothes, often thin and fanciful, are a false skin that does not share in our life and can be stripped off without fatal injury. Our thicker garments, worn constantly, are like a plant's inner tissue. But our shirts are our true bark, which cannot be stripped all round without destroying the man. I believe that every race wears some equivalent of the shirt at certain seasons. A man should dress so simply that he can lay his hands on himself in the dark. He should live so compactly and so prepared that, if an enemy takes the town, he can walk out of the gate empty-handed and untroubled, like the old philosopher. One thick garment usually serves as well as three thin ones, and cheap clothing is readily available. A thick coat costs five dollars and lasts as many years; thick trousers cost two dollars, cowhide boots a dollar and a half, a summer hat a quarter of a dollar, and a winter cap sixty-two and a half cents, or a better one can be made at home for next to nothing. Where, then, is the man so poor that, clothed in such a suit earned by his own labour, he will not find wise men to do him reverence?
